segments.en: Mauri! That's hello in Kiribati, and first, a little secret: the name is said Kiribas, because in the local language the letters t and i together make an s sound.

Now picture this. When the new year arrives, some of these islands are among the very first places on Earth to see it. On Kiritimati, also called Christmas Island, the sun of each new day rises before almost anywhere else.

Kiribati is made of thirty-three islands, most of them coral atolls, scattered across a huge stretch of the central Pacific Ocean. It is the only country with islands in all four hemispheres, north, south, east and west.
An atoll is a ring of low, sandy islands around a calm lagoon. On one side, gentle turquoise water. On the other, the deep blue ocean and the roar of waves on the reef.
Most people live on Tarawa, in the Gilbert Islands, where the government is based. Homes are often open-sided, with thatched roofs of pandanus leaves that let the sea breeze drift through.

At the centre of every village stands the maneaba, a great meeting house with a tall, steep roof. Here people gather to talk, celebrate, settle questions and share feasts, and everyone has a traditional place to sit.

The sea is the pantry. Families fish from canoes and from the reef, then eat their catch with coconut, breadfruit and pandanus fruit. A special crop is babai, a giant swamp taro grown in pits and saved for celebrations.

Kiribati dancing is striking to watch. Dancers hold their arms outstretched and move their heads with sharp, bird-like turns, copying the frigatebird, which also flies across the national flag above a rising sun.
The Phoenix Islands, in the middle of the group, are surrounded by one of the largest marine protected areas on the planet, a safe home for sharks, turtles, seabirds and coral.
The I-Kiribati people, as they are called, were skilled navigators, crossing open water by reading the stars, the swell and the flight of birds. Canoe building and sailing are still treasured skills.
Because the islands rise only a little above the waves, people here care deeply about the ocean and the climate, and their voices are heard around the world when leaders talk about rising seas.
Ko rabwa, thank you for visiting! Now sail south-west across the Pacific to more atolls and lagoons, where Tuvalu is waiting.
